title: Learning to swim at fifteen
paragraphs: I grew up within sight of the sea, and I could not swim. In a fishing town this is more common than you might think, but it was still something I hid. When my friends went to the beach, I offered to watch their bags. I became very good at finding reasons to stay on the sand.

When I was fifteen, our school announced that a swimming test would be part of a sports programme. I spent a week planning how to avoid it. In the end, I told my cousin Nur, who had been teaching children at the local pool. She did not laugh. She only asked what time I finished school, and told me to bring a towel.

The first lesson was the most embarrassing hour of my life. I stood in water up to my waist while children half my age splashed past me. Nur made me do nothing except put my face in the water and breathe out. I hated it, and I told her so. She said that was fine, and that I should come back on Thursday.

Progress was slow, and it was not smooth. For three weeks I could float on some days and not on others. What finally changed was not my body but my idea of what I was doing. I had been treating every lesson as a test that I might fail. Nur kept treating it as ordinary practice, and after a while I began to do the same.

I passed the school test, though nobody would have called it elegant. What stays with me is less the swimming than the months before it. I had spent years protecting a secret that took one short conversation to end. There are still things I avoid, and I am sure there always will be. But now, when I notice myself looking for reasons to stay on the sand, I usually know what I am doing.
